intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia-51 (SPG51) is caused by homozygous mutation in the AP4E1 gene (607244) on chromosome 15q21.2.

checks.claim: Autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia-51 (SPG51) is caused by homozygous mutation in the AP4E1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: These results suggest that both patients display autosomal recessive AP4E1 deficiency, due to an almost complete loss of expression of the AP-4 complex.
checks.explanation: Paper identifies homozygous AP4E1 mutation causing AR disease; AP4E1 classified as SPG51.

checks.evidence_quote: We identified a 139 kb (minimum) to 222 kb (maximum) homozygous deletion of chromosome 15q21.2 that includes the 5′ end of two genes: AP4E1
checks.explanation: The deleted region at 15q21.2 includes AP4E1.

paragraphs.text: SPG51 is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by deficiency of the adaptor protein complex-4 (AP-4). It is characterized by early infantile hypotonia that progresses to spasticity of the lower limbs or of all 4 limbs, profound or severe intellectual disability, absent or very limited speech, inability to walk, microcephaly, stereotypic laughter, and drooling (Moreno-De-Luca et al., 2011; Abou Jamra et al., 2011; Kong et al., 2013). Some patients have seizures, short stature or growth retardation, and facial dysmorphism (Moreno-De-Luca et al., 2011; Abou Jamra et al., 2011; Kong et al., 2013).

checks.evidence_quote: Adaptor protein complex 4 deficiency causes severe autosomal-recessive intellectual disability, progressive spastic paraplegia, shy character, and short stature.
checks.explanation: The title states that AP4 deficiency causes a severe neurodevelopmental phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) proposed the term 'AP-4 deficiency syndrome' for the autosomal recessive disorder caused by disruption of any of the 4 subunits of AP-4. They first described the disorder in their family as a form of spastic tetraplegic cerebral palsy. Kong et al. (2013) regarded AP-4 deficiency syndrome as a subtype of hereditary spastic paraplegia and noted that AP4E1-related disease is classified as SPG51.

paragraphs.text: Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) reported a consanguineous Palestinian-Jordanian family in which 2 sibs had a disorder described as cerebral palsy. Both were born at term after uneventful pregnancies. The female sib (IV-4) had microcephaly and hypotonia at birth, which progressed to spastic tetraplegia with hyperreflexia and generalized hypertonia by the first year of life. She never developed speech or independent walking. She had been wheelchair-bound since 5 years of age, which was also when generalized tonic-clonic seizures began. On examination at age 23 years she had microcephaly (-3 SD), profoundly impaired cognitive ability, deficient adaptive skills (age equivalents less than 1 year), drooling, and outbursts of stereotypic laughter. Dysmorphic features included bitemporal narrowing, a long narrow face with a prominent pointed chin, downslanting palpebral fissures, a long nose with a wide nasal ridge, a short philtrum with an everted full upper vermilion, prominent antehelix of the ears, and facial hypotonia. Brain MRI showed ventriculomegaly, cortical and cerebellar atrophy, reduced hippocampal volume, and diffuse white matter loss that was more pronounced in the frontal region and corpus callosum. EEG showed generalized theta slowing of the background. Her brother (IV-5) had microcephaly and hypotonia postnatally, and developmental delay was evident by the first year of life. He acquired some dysarthric words but never normal speech. He walked with support until increasing spasticity made him wheelchair-dependent by age 9 years. Seizures began as staring spells and became generalized tonic-clonic at age 15. At age 22 years he had spastic tetraplegia with hypertonia and hyperreflexia, stereotypic laughter, drooling, jerky nystagmus, and severe cognitive deficits. His dysmorphic features and EEG were very similar to his sister's, and head CT showed moderate ventriculomegaly with slightly prominent cisterns. Neither sib had sphincter control, and both had a Babinski sign and normal eye and hearing evaluations.

paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2013) reported identical twin girls born to first-cousin Moroccan parents. The pregnancy had no complications, but neonatal asphyxia was noted at delivery. At 3 years of age the twins had marked developmental retardation, with microcephaly (head circumference -2 SD and -2.5 SD), an inability to walk unaided, abnormal speech, and abnormal circadian development. They smiled or laughed for no obvious reason and had abnormal drooling. Both had early infantile hypotonia and spastic paraplegia of the lower extremities, without hypertonia, hyperreflexia, or Babinski sign. Other pseudobulbar signs included a jaw jerk and gag reflex. Both lacked sphincter control and had no seizures. They had short stature, low body weight, and a facial gestalt with a prominent bulbous nose, wide mouth, and coarse features. EEG showed diffuse slow waves, and CT showed atrophy of the inferior vermis with cortical atrophy. One twin had slight myopia and astigmatism and conductive deafness on the left side; the other had slight astigmatism. The twins were diagnosed with type I complex hereditary spastic paraplegia. Both also had mycobacterial disease (see Other Features).

paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2013) reported that the Moroccan twins with AP4E1-related spastic paraplegia had been vaccinated with BCG a few days after birth. Both developed unilaterally enlarged and inflamed axillary lymph nodes at 9 months of age. The nodes were removed surgically, and biopsy showed acid-fast bacilli, consistent with mycobacterial infection. Neither twin had had another episode of mycobacterial infection by age 3 years. Counts of neutrophils, monocytes, B cells, T-cell subsets, and NK cells were normal, as were immunoglobulins and complement. The IL-12/IFN-gamma circuit, IFN-gamma-induced GAF DNA-binding activity, and superoxide production were also normal. Exome data showed no causal mutation in known genes for Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (MSMD). A heterozygous IFNGR1 variant (Q190R) and a heterozygous IL12RB2 variant (K768N) were judged to have no functional effect. Kong et al. (2013) proposed that the AP4E1 mutation was the most likely cause of the mycobacterial disease in these patients. They noted that mycobacterial disease had not been reported in other patients with AP-4 deficiency.

paragraphs.text: Kong et al. (2018) later studied Moroccan monozygotic twin sisters born to first-cousin parents who had hereditary spastic paraplegia due to a homozygous R1105X mutation in AP4E1. Both twins had BCG disease, presenting as axillary lymphadenitis at 9 months of age. By whole-exome sequencing and genome-wide linkage analysis, Kong et al. (2018) identified a homozygous splice site mutation in the SPPL2A gene (c.733+1G-A) in both twins. They concluded that the twins had MSMD caused by autosomal recessive SPPL2a deficiency.

paragraphs.text: The transmission pattern of SPG51 in the family reported by Moreno-De-Luca et al. (2011) was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. Both affected sibs were homozygous for a deletion. FISH showed that the mother and an older unaffected sister were heterozygous carriers, and a younger unaffected sib did not carry the deletion. No paternal sample was available. SNRPN methylation analysis in both patients showed biparental inheritance of chromosome 15, so the father was inferred to be a carrier.

(2013) identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the AP4E1 gene, resulting in an arg1105-to-ter (R1105X) substitution.
